data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"Ownership-based allocation does not systematically suppress cross-cutting explanations; the observed failure of an owning lineage to use a rival's primitive is a local efficiency loss, not systemic suppression, unless the ratio of rival-success events to owning-success events exceeds a structural threshold across a run.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the owning lineage's vocabulary is a universal grammar deriving all rival primitives, S=0 and suppression is absent by definition.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"If rival lineages are not actually rival (they share the same primitive set), S=0 and the test is invalid.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the cost of broadcasting to all lineages exceeds the value of the cross-cutting explanations found, the allocation is efficient even if S/(S+E) is high.","eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Suppression implies a structural or policy-driven barrier preventing cross-lineage primitive transfer. Efficiency implies a local cost-benefit optimization: the owning lineage is chosen because it is heuristically closest, and its failure to use a rival primitive reflects search depth limits, not a barrier. The distinction is quantitative. Following the cross-cutting suppression test: broadcast a fixed problem set P to all lineages. Count S = rival-success-with-novel-primitive events, E = owning-success/rival-failure events. A ratio S/(S+E) > 0.3 indicates suppression; a lower ratio indicates efficiency.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
